line: Jung's statements on the anima: the name, the figure in a man's dreams and projections, and why she cannot be integrated.

sections.title: The name and the figure
sections.line: CW9ii and CW9i: why Jung chose the word anima, and how the figure appears in a man.

quotes.quote: I have suggested instead the term "anima," as indicating something specific, for which the expression "soul" is too general and too vague.
Much of the fear which the female sex arouses in men is due to the projection of the anima-image.
The anima lives beyond all categories, and can therefore dispense with blame as well as with praise.
Besides this ambivalence, the anima also has "occult" connections with "mysteries," with the world of darkness in general, and for that reason she often has a religious tinge.

sections.title: Her work in the psyche
sections.line: CW9i and CW9ii: the anima as the master-piece after the shadow, as a connecting link, and as what stays unassimilated.

quotes.quote: Thus the anima is and remains the representative of that part of the unconscious which can never be assimilated into a humanly attainable whole.
The recognition of the anima gives rise, in a man, to a triad, one third of which is transcendent: the masculine subject, the opposing feminine subject, and the transcendent anima.
The star stands for the transcendent totality, the demon for the animus, who, like the anima, is the connecting link between conscious and unconscious.
The animus corresponds to the paternal Logos just as the anima corresponds to the maternal Eros.
